content: 1. Congenital anemia due to fetal blood loss is a condition where the fetus experiences significant blood loss, leading to anemia present at birth. 2. Other congenital anemias, not classified elsewhere, include cases of anemia present at birth without a specific underlying cause identified. 3. Congenital anemia, not otherwise specified (NOS), refers to anemia diagnosed in the newborn without further specification of its etiology. 4. Other specified perinatal hematological disorders encompass a range of blood-related conditions affecting the newborn during the perinatal period, which are specifically identified but not classified under other categories. 5. Unspecified perinatal hematological disorders refer to blood-related conditions in the newborn during the perinatal period where the exact nature of the disorder is not determined. 6. Congenital renal failure in newborns, also referred to as uremia of the newborn, is a condition where the kidneys fail to function properly from birth. 7. Termination of pregnancy affecting the fetus and newborn refers to complications arising from the termination of pregnancy that impact the fetus or newborn. 8. Complications of intrauterine procedures, not classified elsewhere, include adverse outcomes resulting from medical interventions performed during pregnancy. 9. Other specified conditions originating in the perinatal period include a variety of disorders that begin during the perinatal period and are specifically identified but not classified under other categories. 10. Unspecified conditions originating in the perinatal period refer to disorders that arise during the perinatal period but lack a specific diagnosis. 11. Disorders related to fetal growth include conditions such as slow fetal growth and fetal malnutrition. 12. Light for gestational age describes infants whose weight is below the 10th percentile for their gestational age, while their length is above the 10th percentile. 13. Small for gestational age refers to infants whose weight and length are both below the 10th percentile for their gestational age. 14. Fetal malnutrition without mention of being light or small for gestational age describes infants who show signs of malnutrition, such as dry, peeling skin and loss of subcutaneous tissue, despite not being classified as light or small for their gestational age. 15. Unspecified slow fetal growth refers to cases of fetal growth retardation where the specific cause or nature of the growth restriction is not identified. 16. Disorders related to short gestation and low birth weight, not classified elsewhere, include conditions where the newborn is affected by prematurity or low birth weight without further specification. 17. Extremely low birth weight refers to infants born with a weight of 999 grams or less. 18. Other low birth weight describes infants born with a weight between 1000 and 2499 grams. 19. Extreme immaturity refers to infants born at less than 28 completed weeks of gestation (less than 196 completed days). 20. Other preterm infants are those born between 28 and 37 completed weeks of gestation (196 to 259 completed days). 21. Disorders related to long gestation and high birth weight include conditions affecting infants born after prolonged gestation or with excessive birth weight. 22. Exceptionally large babies are those with a birth weight of 4500 grams or more. 23. Other heavy-for-gestational-age infants are those with a birth weight above the 90th percentile for their gestational age or 4000 grams or more at term. 24. Post-term infants, not heavy for gestational age, are those born after 42 completed weeks of gestation (294 days or more) without being classified as heavy or large for their gestational age. 25. Birth trauma includes injuries sustained by the newborn during the process of birth. 26. Intracranial laceration and hemorrhage due to birth injury include conditions such as subdural hemorrhage, cerebral hemorrhage, intraventricular hemorrhage, subarachnoid hemorrhage, and tentorial tears caused by birth trauma. 27. Other birth injuries to the central nervous system include cerebral edema, brain damage, facial nerve injury, cranial nerve injury, and spinal cord injury resulting from birth trauma. 28. Birth injuries to the scalp include cephalhematoma, chignon, epicranial subaponeurotic hemorrhage, bruising, and injuries caused by monitoring devices during delivery. 29. Birth injuries to the skeleton include fractures of the skull, femur, clavicle, and other long bones, as well as injuries to other parts of the skeleton. 30. Birth injuries to the peripheral nervous system include conditions such as Erb paralysis, Klumpke paralysis, phrenic nerve paralysis, and other brachial plexus injuries caused by birth trauma. 31. Other birth injuries include damage to the liver, spleen, sternomastoid muscle, eye, face, external genitalia, and subcutaneous fat due to birth trauma. 32. Intrauterine hypoxia refers to oxygen deprivation experienced by the fetus while in the uterus. 33. Birth asphyxia describes a condition where the newborn experiences oxygen deprivation during birth, leading to potential complications. 34. Disorders of muscle tone in the newborn include transient neonatal myasthenia gravis, congenital hypertonia, congenital hypotonia (floppy baby syndrome), and other unspecified muscle tone disorders. 35. Congenital malformations include a wide range of structural abnormalities present at birth, affecting various systems such as the cardiovascular, respiratory, digestive, musculoskeletal, and genitourinary systems. 36. Specific congenital malformations include conditions such as Down syndrome, cleft lip, cleft palate, congenital ichthyosis, and other syndromes caused by known exogenous factors. 37. Placental transfusion syndromes refer to abnormalities in placental or cord function, such as twin-to-twin transfusion, which can result in complications for the fetus or newborn.
